items.q: Why did I get lymphedema after my cancer surgery?
items.a: Lymphedema is swelling that happens when lymph fluid cannot drain properly after lymph nodes are removed or damaged. Surgery that takes out nodes in the armpit, groin, or pelvis interrupts the drainage pathway, and radiation to the same area can add scarring. Fluid then collects in the arm, leg, breast, or trunk. Risk rises with the number of nodes removed, but many people who have node surgery never develop it.

items.q: How soon after surgery does lymphedema usually start?
items.a: Lymphedema most often appears in the first two to three years after surgery, but it can start months or even decades later. Some swelling right after an operation is normal and settles as healing finishes. Swelling that begins later, builds slowly, and does not go down overnight is more concerning. Because the risk never fully disappears, most cancer teams ask you to keep measuring or watching the limb long term.

items.q: What are the first signs I should watch for?
items.a: The earliest signs are usually a feeling of heaviness, tightness, or fullness before any visible swelling. Rings, watches, sleeves, or shoes may start to feel snug, and the skin can look slightly puffy at the end of the day. Some people notice aching or reduced flexibility in the wrist or ankle. Report these changes early, because treatment started at this stage often controls the swelling far more easily.

items.q: Will lymphedema ever go away completely?
items.a: Lymphedema is usually a long-term condition that can be controlled well but is rarely cured. Mild, early swelling sometimes settles almost completely with compression and exercise, and many people keep their limb close to normal size for years. Left untreated, however, the tissue can thicken and the swelling becomes harder to reverse. Think of it as a condition you manage daily, much like blood pressure or diabetes.

items.q: What does lymphedema treatment actually involve?
items.a: The standard treatment is complete decongestive therapy, given by a trained lymphedema therapist. It combines manual lymphatic drainage, compression bandaging, specific exercises, and careful skin care. An intensive phase of near-daily sessions reduces the limb over two to four weeks, then a maintenance phase uses a fitted garment at home. CancerFax can help you locate a certified therapist near you or at your treatment hospital abroad.

items.q: Do I have to wear a compression sleeve for the rest of my life?
items.a: Most people need compression long term, but not always all day and not always the same garment. A therapist measures you for a flat-knit or circular-knit sleeve or stocking and replaces it every four to six months as the elastic tires. Many patients wear it during the day, for exercise, and on flights, then switch to a softer night garment. Your therapist can adjust the schedule as your limb stabilizes.

items.q: Can I exercise or lift weights with lymphedema?
items.a: Yes, exercise is now recommended rather than avoided, including gradual strength training. Trials in breast cancer survivors found that slow, progressive weight lifting did not worsen lymphedema and often reduced flare-ups. The rules are to start light, add load slowly, wear your compression garment while training, and stop if the limb feels heavy or aches afterwards. Ask your therapist to review your program before you begin any new routine.

items.q: Is it safe to fly, or will the flight make my swelling worse?
items.a: Flying is generally safe, and most people with treated lymphedema travel without problems. Cabin pressure is lower than at ground level, which can allow slightly more fluid to collect, so wearing a well-fitted compression garment for the whole flight is the usual advice. Move your fingers, ankles, and shoulders often, drink water, and avoid heavy carry-on bags on the affected side. Get your garment checked before long journeys.

items.q: How do I stop my swollen arm or leg from getting infected?
items.a: Keep the skin clean, moisturized, and unbroken, because infection is the main danger in a swollen limb. Use gloves for gardening and washing up, treat cuts and insect bites promptly with antiseptic, and avoid very hot baths or saunas. Call your doctor the same day if the skin turns red, hot, or painful, or you develop fever, since cellulitis needs antibiotics quickly and can worsen the swelling permanently.

items.q: Is there surgery that can fix lymphedema?
items.a: Surgery can help selected patients but does not replace compression for most people. Lymphaticovenous anastomosis joins tiny lymph vessels to nearby veins and suits earlier, softer swelling, while vascularized lymph node transfer moves healthy nodes into the affected area. Liposuction is used when the limb has turned fatty and firm. Suitability depends on imaging and duration, so ask your surgical team; CancerFax can help arrange specialist opinions in India or China.
